slides.title: Today
text: Today
How to derive graph convolutional networks (GCNs) in a principled way?
Convolutions are linear operators with special properties.
• Similarly, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs)
with special contraints derived from 2D image / 1D time data.
• How to generalize the “special constraints” to graphs?

slides.title: Towards Graph Convolutional Networks
text: Towards Graph Convolutional Networks
Convolution is a fundamental operator on two functions (signals) 𝐟 and 𝐠
that produces a third function 𝐟 ∗ 𝐠.
• Image signal processing allows to define convolutional neural networks,
where 𝑓(𝑖, 𝑗) is an image “signal” and 𝑔(𝑖, 𝑗) is a kernel function.
How to derive graph signal processing and graph convolution?

slides.title: The Big Picture
text: The Big Picture
Signal processing deals with discrete-time signal 𝐟 = [𝑓 0 , … , 𝑓 𝑁 − 1 ].
Extended to graph signal 𝐟 = 𝑓 𝑛 : 𝑛 ∈ 𝑉 for vertex set 𝑉.
Time signal is just a graph signal associated with a directed cyclic graph.
• We first describe the signal processing for directed line graph,
then generalize to arbitrary graphs.

slides.title: The Big Picture
text: The Big Picture
Fourier transformation is a mapping from the “real” space to the frequency space,
decomposing a real-valued signal into coefficients of the Fourier basis.
• How to derive the graph Fourier basis and the associated Fourier transformation?
Then convolution can be expressed as element-wise modifications in the Fourier space.
• Filtering is a special convolution that masks out the coefficients.

slides.title: Limits of Graph Signal Processing Perspective
text: Limits of Graph Signal Processing Perspective
Deriving graph convolution from the signal processing perspective is persuasive,
but it does not align with the problem where graphs vary with input.
Here, we consider alternative (and more general) definition of convolutions:
any linear operator that is equivariant to a given set of group actions.

slides.title: Equivariant Linear Operators
text: Equivariant Linear Operators
An alterantive definition of convolution: equivariant linear operators.
• For examples, typical convolution for 1D, 2D, and 3D are
equivariant to translation operators.
Can we fully characterize the space of linear operators
that are equivariant to permutation?

slides.title: Shift Equivariant Linear Operators
text: Shift Equivariant Linear Operators
Let’s start again by the 1D discrete-time convolution case.
Here, the set of transformations (group) is constructed
from iteratively applying the shift operator, i.e.,
• Time shift is done by 𝑥 ↦ 𝐴𝑥
What we want is the convolution matrix 𝐶 satisfying:
𝐴𝐶𝑥 = 𝐶𝐴𝑥.
When 𝐴𝐶 = 𝐶𝐴, we say 𝐶 commutes with 𝐴.
• Commuting matrices share the eigenvectors.

slides.title: Shift Equivariant Linear Operators
text: Shift Equivariant Linear Operators
A matrix commutes with the time-shift operator
if and only if it is a circulant matrix,
i.e., it defines convolution in time domain.
This is extended to saying that
a linear operator (matrix multiplication)
is shift-equivariant if and only if
it is a convolution.
